notable_absence.finding: dependsOnService - the one composition predicate the registry has, and the one it minted on this very subtree in round 1 - turns out to be too coarse for the page it came from. It has no way to express (a) an ALTERNATIVE dependency ('either the Index Service or the Search Service'), (b) a per-OPERATION dependency (Scan goes to one service, Fetch to another) as opposed to a whole-service one, or (c) the difference between a hard prerequisite and a runtime delegation. The Search Service is the acid test: this page's lede names exactly two hard dependencies (Index, Data), and services.md's example agrees, yet the Query Execution section has the Query Service routing Scans to the Search Service. Under dependsOnService alone you must either lose that fact or promote Search to a hard dependency and contradict the lede. I minted mayDelegateOperationTo and recorded both arms of the disjunction rather than choose. Separately: this page describes a DATAFLOW SEQUENCE (receive -> parse -> plan -> scan -> fetch -> join -> filter/aggregate/project/sort -> offset/limit -> stream) and the registry has no ordering predicate whatsoever, so the sequence itself is unextractable - I collapsed it into one hasExecutionPhase relation pointing at a flat scheme, which loses the ordering. Same gap flagged on data-service.md and index-service.md; three of five pages in this batch hit it, so it is the batch's second-clearest structural finding after the missing part-whole predicate. NOTHING WAS DROPPED for lack of evidence.

cross_component_finding: (1) OPTIMIZER IDENTITY, unresolved and worth SME attention: this page's Optimizer 'evaluates available execution paths, so determining the path of lowest latency'. The registry's n1ql:cost-based-optimizer (recurrence 15, one of its best-attested concepts) is a statistics-driven optimizer requiring a prior UPDATE STATISTICS run (registry predicate requiresPriorExecutionOf). Nothing on this page mentions cost or statistics, and nothing on the CBO pages says the CBO IS the Optimizer component rather than a mode of it. So the canonical conceptual page for the Query Service does not connect to the ontology's richest Query-Service concept at all. I minted a separate query-service:optimizer and am flagging it rather than merging - exactly the situation the registry's collision notes exist for. (2) The lede's dependency claim and the Query Execution section's delegation claim are in tension within one page (see notable_absence). (3) The 'Data Stores' component reveals that the Query Service can read non-Couchbase sources ('the store for the local filesystem') - a capability with no other trace anywhere in the ontology after nine rounds and ~540 pages. (4) Architecture is again carried by a PNG (queryServiceArchitecture.png) plus prose that partially restates it; the Figure 2 execution-sequence SVG encodes degree-of-parallelism per operator ('the number of boxes within an operation block represents the degree of parallelism'), which is unextractable from a Markdown snapshot by construction.
cross_product_finding: The Query Service is the most heavily extracted subject in the whole corpus - n1ql:query-service-rest-api (12), 30+ n1ql:* statement concepts, request/node/cluster-level settings - and essentially none of it attaches here. The reference tree documents the Query Service as an API and a language; this page documents it as a process with listeners, a planner and a thread-level parallelism model. The only two joins between the two views in this record are usesPort (to the same port:8093 that the REST API pages already cited) and n1ql:scan-consistency, which arrives here under a third label ('_consistency-levels_'), abstracted away from both the four-valued server setting and the Java SDK's two-member enum. That third label is a small but real vindication of keeping those as one concept with recorded label variance rather than splitting them. Capella's tree, by contrast, exposes none of this: it has capella:query-tab and capella:data-api as access surfaces onto the Query Service and never describes the service's internals, so nothing in the Capella-derived vocabulary can attach to any concept minted on this page.
